# A map of the bacteria

> *Lectures name bacteria by group: Gram-positive cocci, Enterobacterales, anaerobes, atypicals. Each
> group is a combination of a few traits, and the combination explains how the group behaves.*

## Reading a group as a set of traits {#sec-map-idea}

[*How bacteria are built and get energy*](../principles/bacteria-build-energy.qmd#sec-bact-toolkit)
gave you a trait toolkit: envelope, shape, relationship with oxygen and growth. Two more traits matter
for whole groups of bacteria. The first is where the organism grows: outside cells, inside or outside
cells, or only inside cells. The second is what it needs in the laboratory: ordinary media, enriched
media, weeks of incubation, or living cells.

A bacterial group can then be described in those terms. Enterobacterales, for example, are
Gram-negative rods that grow with or without oxygen, ferment sugars, and live in the gut. Once you can
read a group this way, its name becomes a summary of how the group lives.

Groups are named in different ways, which is part of what makes the list confusing. Some names come
from the family tree (Enterobacterales). Some describe a single trait (anaerobes, spiral bacteria).
Some describe a failure of the usual laboratory methods (fastidious, atypical). The map below puts them
all on the same footing.

Sort the table by *Oxygen*, then by *Envelope*, using the column headings. Groups that sound unrelated

## Metabolism predicts habitat {#sec-map-habitat}

Two groups on the map are both Gram-negative rods, yet one lives in the gut and the other in water and
soil. The difference lies in how they make ATP.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-ecoli-pseudomonas.yml"></div>

The same reasoning explains the **fastidious** bacteria. Over evolutionary time, a bacterium that lives
on a rich host can lose the genes for making nutrients the host already supplies, and then depends on
finding them. *Haemophilus*, for example, needs two factors found inside red blood cells, so the
laboratory grows it on agar made with blood heated until the cells lyse: **chocolate agar**, named for
its brown colour. "Fastidious" therefore describes lost biosynthesis.

The **Gram-negative cocci**, the *Neisseria* species, show the same logic from another angle. They live
only in humans and die quickly outside the body, drying out in air and needing enriched media in the
laboratory. A fragile organism can spread only by close contact between people, which is how both
major *Neisseria* species spread.

## Worked example: why "atypical"? {#sec-map-atypicals}

The **atypical** bacteria are three genera, *Mycoplasma*, *Chlamydia* and *Rickettsia*, that are not
closely related. They are grouped because the usual microbiology toolkit fails on them. The name comes
from the clinic: the chest infections some of them cause did not look like typical bacterial
pneumonia, and did not respond to penicillin.

A more useful question than "what are the atypicals?" is "why does the toolkit fail on them?" There are
two different reasons, and each predicts a great deal.

| | *Mycoplasma* | *Chlamydia* | *Rickettsia* |
|---|---|---|---|
| What is unusual | No cell wall at all | Lives only inside host cells; two-form life cycle | Lives only inside host cells, free in the cytoplasm |
| Envelope | Membrane only, stiffened with sterols | Gram-negative type, with very little peptidoglycan | Gram-negative type |
| Energy | Makes its own ATP | Imports ATP from the host cell | Imports ATP from the host cell |
| Transmission | Respiratory droplets | Direct contact, sexual or eye to eye | Bites of ticks, lice, fleas or mites |
| Gram stain | Nothing to read | Too small, and hidden inside cells | Stains poorly |
| Laboratory growth | Slowly, on media enriched with sterols | Only in living cells | Only in living cells |

Start with the first reason, the missing wall, and predict what follows from it.

<div data-island="microbe-profile" data-src="/diagrams/profile-m-pneumoniae.yml"></div>

*Chlamydia* also fails the Gram stain and will not grow on agar, but for a different reason.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-mycoplasma-chlamydia.yml"></div>

::: {.callout-important}
## A common idea, corrected: "atypical means rare or unimportant"
"Atypical" describes the laboratory toolkit, not how often these bacteria cause disease. *Chlamydia
trachomatis* is one of the most common sexually transmitted bacteria in the world, and *Mycoplasma
pneumoniae* is a common cause of pneumonia in children and young adults. Standard stains and cultures
miss them, so laboratories usually detect them by their nucleic acid.
:::

In the respiratory and genitourinary blocks you will meet these organisms again, with the diseases they
cause, how those diseases are diagnosed and how they are treated. Most of those facts follow from the
two ideas on this page: no wall, or growth only inside cells.

## How the group chapters work {#sec-map-template}

Each chapter that follows takes one group from the map and uses the same layout.

| Part of the chapter | What it gives you |
|---|---|
| The group in one sentence | The group's row on the map, as a description |
| Sorting key | The few traits that separate members of the group, and what each trait means |
| Main organisms | Two or three organisms, each with a full profile card and its patterns of harm: how a mechanism leads to a kind of damage, with one example |
| Contrast pairs | The organisms most easily confused, side by side |
| Supporting organisms | One table row each |
| Later in the course | Where the organ-system blocks add diseases, diagnosis and treatment |
